title: How to Generate Three Differentiated Worksheets From One Lesson Using AI
author: Phillip Alcock
summary: Phillip Alcock gives teachers a step-by-step workflow for turning one master lesson into three differentiated worksheets (approaching, meeting, exceeding) using Claude Desktop's Cowork mode. He frames the problem as time rather than theory: teachers know differentiation matters but cannot rewrite every lesson three ways on a Sunday evening. The guide covers setting up a dedicated folder, writing a prompt that fixes filenames and specifies vocabulary, scaffolding, task type and assessment format per level, granting file permissions, comparing outputs, and refining one file at a time. He sketches uses in humanities, maths and science and suggests saving the prompt as a reusable skill. He is honest that output quality tracks the quality of the master lesson and that formatting can vary across operating systems. The opening and closing carry membership promotion, but the body is a concrete, classroom-specific build guide.
points: The pitch is that differentiation fails on time, not belief, and the workflow compresses a long evening of rewriting into a few minutes.
The prompt does the pedagogical work: it names exact files and spells out vocabulary, scaffolding, task and assessment demands for each level.
The learning objectives stay constant across the three worksheets while the path to them changes, which is the check the teacher should apply to the outputs.
Targeted follow-up prompts on a single file are faster than starting over, and the prompt can be saved as a reusable skill.
Results depend on a well-structured master lesson, so teacher expertise in lesson design remains the limiting factor.
quotes: You know differentiation matters. Every PD session you’ve attended in the last five years has told you that. The problem was never the theory behind it and always about the time it takes to do this.. for .. every.. lesson.

Claude’s Cowork mode can read your master lesson file, apply a differentiation framework you define, and save three separate Word documents to your desktop. The whole process takes about seven minutes once you know the steps.
The filenames matter more than you’d think. By specifying worksheet-approaching.docx rather than leaving the naming to Claude, you guarantee you can identify each file immediately.
Your teaching expertise drives the vocabulary and scaffolding descriptions. Claude follows specific instructions well, so if you want word banks in the Approaching version, say that.

What you’re checking for: do all three worksheets share the same learning objectives? They should, that’s the whole point of differentiation. The learning goals stay constant while the path to reaching them changes.

In each case, the teacher’s expertise goes into designing the master lesson and writing the differentiation prompt. Cowork handles the mechanical production of three separate, well-formatted documents.

Output quality depends on the quality of your master lesson. If your source file is a loose collection of notes with inconsistent formatting, Cowork will do its best, but the worksheets will reflect that unevenness.
